Part 6 of Block Diffusion RooflinesPrevious: 5 · ExercisesNext: 7 · The measurement stack

Proposition 1 takes two kinds of input that Parts 1–5 do not measure: the rates of the accelerator, which we take from its datasheet, and the experts each pass touches, which we take from the assumption that tokens route independently (A5). In this chapter, we measure both on one H200, for DiffusionGemma and Gemma 4. We will see that the measured ceilings lower the bound at every point, while routing moves it by the largest factors, upward at small batch and downward at large batch.

What one H200 sustains

The datasheet of an H200 announces 989 TFLOP/s in BF16, 1,979 in FP8 and 4.8 TB/s. These rates assume its 1,980 MHz boost clock, and they say nothing about attention. In practice, a kernel that keeps the tensor cores (the matrix-multiply units) busy draws power until it reaches the 700 W cap, and the GPU then lowers its clock. Hence, we measure the rates a kernel can reach, in the manner of the Empirical Roofline Toolkit (Lo et al., 2014): several benchmarks per rate, with the clock and the power logged during each.

Definition 5Empirical ceilings and empirical roofline

In short. The empirical ceiling of a rate is the highest value measured on this GPU (for attention, a sustained reference rate); the empirical roofline of a component is \(\max(F_c/\hat\pi_c,\ Q_c/\hat\beta)\) at those ceilings.

The empirical ceiling of a rate is the highest value that its benchmarks reach on random data, except for attention, whose ceiling is a sustained reference rate:

  • \(\hat\pi_{\mathrm{fp8}}\), \(\hat\pi_{\mathrm{bf16}}\): GEMMs (general matrix multiplications) of 11 shapes from \(2048^3\) to \(32768 \times 4096 \times 4096\), each run for 0.5 s, a short burst of an \(8192^3\) GEMM, and the model's own projections at 1 to 16,384 tokens, replayed from CUDA graphs1 in bursts of about 2 ms;
  • \(\hat\pi_{\mathrm{attn}}\): FlashAttention 3 at head dimension 128 on long square sequences, sustained for 0.5 s. Attention kernels at other shapes can exceed it in short bursts,2 so for attention the ceiling is a sustained reference rate rather than a maximum;
  • \(\hat\beta\): reads and copies of 0.25–8 GB buffers.

A component \(c\) of a pass (experts, dense GEMMs, window attention, global attention, vocabulary head) with \(F_c\) FLOPs and \(Q_c\) bytes of memory traffic has the empirical roofline

\[ \tau_c = \max\Bigl(\frac{F_c}{\hat\pi_c},\ \frac{Q_c}{\hat\beta}\Bigr), \]

with \(\hat\pi_c\) the ceiling of its kind: FP8 GEMM for dense layers and experts, attention for attention, BF16 GEMM for the vocabulary head. The empirical roofline of a step of decoder \(X\) is the sum over its components, \(\tau_X = \sum_c \tau_c\), the kernel-by-kernel rule of Part 1.

Three findings determine how we use the ceilings.

  • Power, not the tensor cores, limits sustained compute. On random data, GEMMs from \(4096^3\) up that run for half a second hold 1,275–1,530 MHz at 675–695 W and reach 700 TFLOP/s in BF16 and 1,336 in FP8. Per clock cycle, the BF16 rate is 0.93 of the datasheet's. Hence, the kernels are close to ideal, and the shortfall is the clock.3 On the other hand, kernels inside the engine run for milliseconds between memory-bound kernels and see higher clocks. This is why the ceiling is the highest rate measured, including the 2 ms bursts.
  • Attention has its own ceiling. FlashAttention 3 sustains 638 TFLOP/s, 13% below a BF16 GEMM at the same clock. We attribute this gap to the softmax between its two matrix products.
  • Small GEMMs are bound by latency. With 64 tokens or fewer, the model's projections other than the vocabulary head take 5–13 µs whatever the batch, and they stream their weights at 0.9–3 TB/s, below \(\hat\beta\). This is the floor of an AR step at small batch.4

In particular, the empirical ceilings lower compute (0.74 of the datasheet in FP8) more than bandwidth (0.90). Therefore, they barely change \(\Gamma\) where both decoders are memory-bound, and they lower it where TD is compute-bound and AR is not.

roofscope/ert.py23 linesHow the sustained rates of Definition 5 are timed: the median over three repeats of the mean time per call over about half a second of back-to-back calls, with the SM clock and the power sampled every 50 ms by nvidia-smi meanwhile. The ceiling is the highest rate of any benchmark, except for attention; the FP8 and BF16 ceilings come from shorter bursts (CUDA-graph replays of about 2 ms, and 20 back-to-back GEMMs).
75def sustained(fn: Callable[[], Any], seconds: float = 0.5, reps: int = 3) -> float:76    """Median over `reps` of the mean time per call over about `seconds` of back-to-back calls."""77    import torch78 79    for _ in range(3):80        fn()81    torch.cuda.synchronize()82    a, b = torch.cuda.Event(enable_timing=True), torch.cuda.Event(enable_timing=True)83    a.record(); fn(); b.record(); b.synchronize()84    one = max(a.elapsed_time(b) / 1e3, 1e-6)85    n = max(3, int(seconds / one))86    ts = []87    for _ in range(reps):88        a.record()89        for _ in range(n):90            fn()91        b.record(); b.synchronize()92        ts.append(a.elapsed_time(b) / 1e3 / n)93    return statistics.median(ts)⋮ 124def measure(fn: Callable[[], Any], seconds: float = 0.5) -> dict[str, Any]:125    with Monitor() as m:126        t = sustained(fn, seconds)127    return {"t": t, **m.summary()}

Which experts a pass touches

The expert weights a pass reads, and hence the linear penalty of Part 2, depend on how many distinct experts its tokens select. Assumption (A5) of Proposition 1 takes the tokens to choose independently and uniformly. Under (A5), \(N\) tokens touch \(U_{E,k}(N) = E\,[1 - (1 - k/E)^N]\) of the \(E = 128\) experts of a layer, each token selecting \(k = 8\). In particular, a canvas of 256 positions then touches all 128 experts even at batch 1. On the other hand, the router's choices can be counted directly: roofscope, our measurement harness, adds a counter to the engine's router, which records, for every pass and MoE layer, how many tokens went to each expert.

roofscope/routing.py17 linesThe routing counter. vLLM's router calls capture in every MoE layer; one Triton kernel adds 1 to counts[step, layer, expert] for each (token, choice), and the last layer advances a step index kept on the GPU. Both kernels are captured into the CUDA graph, so the timed passes are counted as well.
30def _rs_routing_hist(ids_ptr, n, counts_ptr, step_ptr, layer_off, step_stride, max_steps, E,31                     BLOCK: tl.constexpr):32    pid = tl.program_id(0)33    offs = pid * BLOCK + tl.arange(0, BLOCK)34    msk = offs < n35    e = tl.load(ids_ptr + offs, mask=msk, other=0).to(tl.int64)36    ok = msk & (e >= 0) & (e < E)  # the router may leave unset ids in dummy warm-up batches37    st = tl.maximum(tl.minimum(tl.load(step_ptr), max_steps - 1), 0).to(tl.int64)38    tl.atomic_add(counts_ptr + st * step_stride + layer_off + tl.where(ok, e, 0), 1, mask=ok)⋮ 54    def capture(self, layer_id: int, topk_ids: torch.Tensor) -> None:55        ids = topk_ids if topk_ids.is_contiguous() else topk_ids.contiguous()56        n = ids.numel()57        if n > 0:58            _rs_routing_hist[(triton.cdiv(n, 1024),)](59                ids, n, self.counts, self.step, layer_id * self.E, self.L * self.E, MAX_STEPS, self.E, BLOCK=1024)60        if layer_id == self.last_layer:61            _rs_routing_step[(1,)](self.step)

Definition 6Measured routing

In short. \(U^{\mathrm{meas}}\) counts the experts a pass actually touches; \(U^{\mathrm{freq}}\) is what independent tokens with the measured popularity would touch; \(N^{\mathrm{eff}}\) is the number of uniformly routed tokens that would touch \(U^{\mathrm{meas}}\).

A pass holds \(N\) tokens: \(N = B\) for an AR step and \(N = Bb\) for a TD pass. For a decoder at batch \(B\) and context \(C\):

  • \(U^{\mathrm{meas}}\) is the number of distinct experts a pass touches in one MoE layer, averaged over the 30 layers and the timed passes; across the three repeats of a point, its median.
  • \(\rho_e\) is the probability that a token selects expert \(e\), estimated per layer from all passes of a run, and \(U^{\mathrm{freq}} = \sum_{e=1}^{E} \bigl[1 - (1 - \rho_e)^N\bigr]\) is the count that \(N\) independent tokens with these frequencies would touch.5
  • \(N^{\mathrm{eff}}\), the effective number of independent tokens, solves \(U_{E,k}(N^{\mathrm{eff}}) = U^{\mathrm{meas}}\): the number of tokens that, routed independently and uniformly, would touch as many experts as the pass does.

Then \(U^{\mathrm{freq}}/U_{E,k}(N)\) measures the effect of uneven expert popularity, and \(U^{\mathrm{meas}}/U^{\mathrm{freq}}\) the effect of dependence between the tokens of a pass. Since the frequencies \(\rho_e\) are pooled over all sequences of a run, the second ratio also contains popularity that differs from one sequence to another.

Both decoders touch fewer experts than independent routing predicts, for different reasons.

Choose the decoder and the context; hover over or tap a batch to read the counts.

Distinct experts per MoE layer and forward pass \(U\), averaged over the 30 layers and the timed passes, against batch size: the median of three repeats with different prompts, and the band spanning them. Dotted: independent tokens with uniform routing (A5), \(U_{E,k}(N)\) of Definition 1. Dashed: independent tokens with each expert's measured popularity (Definition 6). The two decoders depart from (A5) in different ways. All counts below are from essay prompts (Part 7).6

  • AR is independent once popularity is counted. The ratio \(U^{\mathrm{meas}}/U^{\mathrm{freq}}\) is 0.98–1.03 at every point. On the other hand, popularity alone removes 35–49% of the experts that uniform routing predicts from batch 8 on. For instance, at batch 64 and context 4k, independent tokens with the measured popularity touch 69 experts, the measured count is 69, and uniform routing predicts 126.
  • TD's experts are also unevenly popular, and its positions are dependent. Popularity removes 7–36% of the uniform count for a canvas: \(U^{\mathrm{freq}}\) is 82–119 of 128 at contexts 1k–16k. In addition, \(U^{\mathrm{meas}}/U^{\mathrm{freq}}\) is 0.76–0.86 at batch 1 and 0.81–0.98 from batch 2 on, at contexts 1k–16k. Per layer, the dependence is strongest in the first five MoE layers: one of them has the lowest ratio at 23 of the 25 measured points, over all contexts (0.49 in the first layer at batch 1 and 1k, against 0.82 on average over layers 6–30).
  • Context barely moves TD's count up to 16k. At batch 16, \(U^{\mathrm{meas}}\) is 104, 106 and 107 at 1k, 4k and 16k, and 84 at 64k, where the generated text degrades.

In particular, at batch 1 a canvas of 256 positions touches 65–74 experts per layer at contexts 1k–16k, i.e., as many as 11 to 13 independent tokens. At batch 64, its 16,384 positions touch as many experts as 37–38 independent tokens would, at contexts 1k–4k. An AR step at batch 64 touches as many as 12 independent tokens: its sequences are independent, but the popular experts take most of the selections.7

Remark 2Proposition 1 at measured routing

In short. Measured routing enters Proposition 1 only through the expert weights each pass reads: the expert penalty becomes \(U^{\mathrm{meas}}_{TD}/U^{\mathrm{meas}}_{AR}\), and AR's intensity changes with them.

Proposition 1 depends on routing only through the expert weights that a pass reads, \(s_wL\,U\,W^e\) bytes for \(L\) MoE layers of \(W^e\) parameters per expert. Replacing (A5) by the measured counts therefore amounts to replacing \(N\) by \(N^{\mathrm{eff}}\) in the weights of both decoders, \(\class{mj-ar}{W_{AR}}(B)\) with \(U^{\mathrm{meas}}_{AR}\) experts per layer and \(\class{mj-td}{W_{TD}}(B)\) with \(U^{\mathrm{meas}}_{TD}\). In particular, the expert penalty of Proposition 3 becomes

\[ \Pi_E = \frac{U_{E,k}(N^{\mathrm{eff}}_{TD})}{U_{E,k}(N^{\mathrm{eff}}_{AR})} = \frac{U^{\mathrm{meas}}_{TD}}{U^{\mathrm{meas}}_{AR}}, \]

and AR's linear intensity \(I_{\mathrm{lin}}(B) = 2BN_{\mathrm{act}}/(s_w\class{mj-ar}{W_{AR}}(B))\) changes with \(\class{mj-ar}{W_{AR}}\), and so do the expert share \(\theta_E\), the parity batch and every threshold of Parts 2–4 that depends on \(\class{mj-ar}{W_{AR}}\) or \(\class{mj-td}{W_{TD}}\), such as \(\class{mj-td}{B^\star_{TD}}\). The FLOPs, the KV-cache bytes and the ceilings are unchanged.

The measured routing moves the linear penalty in opposite directions at small and at large batch:

  • Batch 1, context 1k: The measured routing lowers the linear penalty from 7.9 to 4.3. Proposition 1 then gives \(\Gamma = 4.3\), against 2.3 under (A5)8 and 7.0 measured. The measured gain is higher still because TD runs closer to its roofline than AR there (Part 9).
  • From batch 8 on, at contexts 1k–16k: The penalty at measured routing is higher than under (A5) (1.85 against 1.13 at batch 32). Indeed, AR's count (33–71 experts at batch 8–64 and contexts 1k–16k) falls further below the prediction of (A5) (52–126) than TD's (97–117 against 128). Proposition 1 then overestimates the gain (2.0 against a measured 1.04 at batch 32), mainly because it leaves out the vocabulary head, which TD evaluates at all 256 positions of every pass; the exact accounting with the head, bound (c) below, gives 1.15. The head, the sampler and self-conditioning together take 24–34% of TD's step at contexts 1k–4k from batch 4 on.

The bound at measured inputs

The exact accounting includes the vocabulary head, activations and the KV cache. We evaluate it pass by pass at each measured point, with the kernel-by-kernel rule. This gives three bounds, plotted in Figure 25, each of which changes one input of the previous one:

  • (a) datasheet rates and independent routing (A5);
  • (b) the empirical ceilings of Definition 5 in place of the datasheet rates;
  • (c) the expert counts measured in the same runs (Definition 6) in place of independent routing.

Roofline bound on \(\Gamma\) against batch, with FP8 weights, at the measured points; each curve changes one input of the previous one. (a) the blogpost's exact accounting with datasheet rates and independent routing (A5); (b) the empirical ceilings of Table 8; (c) the expert counts measured in the same runs. The measured ceilings lower the bound at every point, by 0.08–0.53; the measured routing then raises it at batch 1–2, changes it by at most 0.06 at batch 4, and lowers it from batch 8 on. Below the parity line AR is faster. Missing points were not measured: the grid keeps \(BC \le 2^{21}\) tokens, and TD's batches at \((32, 64\text{k})\) and \((64, 16\text{k})\) did not fit in memory. The batch axis is logarithmic: the measured sizes 1, 2, 4, …, 64 are equally spaced.

  • Ceilings, (a) to (b). At batch 1, the roofline bound keeps 0.88–0.97 of its value, lowest at 64k. From batch 8 on, where TD is compute-bound and AR is not, it keeps 0.76–0.88.
  • Routing, (b) to (c). At batch 1, the bound rises by a factor of 1.4–1.6. From batch 32 on, it falls to 0.68–0.78 of (b). At contexts 1k–4k, the batch at which AR overtakes TD moves from beyond 64 to between 32 and 64. In addition, up to 16k the bound now falls with the batch from batch 1, whereas bound (a) rose up to batch 4–8.

To summarise, the measured ceilings lower the bound at every point, by factors of 0.76–0.97. On the other hand, routing moves it by the largest factors, from 1.6 at batch 1 to 0.68 at batch 32, and in both directions:

  • Small batch: A canvas touches fewer experts than (A5) predicts, which favours TD.
  • Large batch: The uneven popularity of experts lowers AR's count further than TD's, which favours AR.

In Part 9, we compare the bound (c) with the measured gain.

Notes

  1. A CUDA graph records the kernels of a pass once and replays them with a single launch (Part 7). ↩
  2. Up to 729 TFLOP/s for FlashAttention 4 at head dimension 256 on the query rows of TD's canvases. ↩
  3. On constant inputs, whose bits do not toggle, the same GEMMs draw about 450 W and run 20% faster. Hence the ceilings are measured on random data. ↩
  4. We tested two GEMM libraries at these shapes, cuBLAS, NVIDIA's matrix-multiply library, and vLLM's kernels written with CUTLASS, NVIDIA's template library for such kernels; neither streams the weights faster. ↩
  5. The term \((1 - \rho_e)^N\) is estimated from the run's counts by a ratio of binomial coefficients, which is unbiased if the run's tokens choose independently. ↩
  6. At context 64k, at most a third of TD's measured canvases are text-like, i.e., have at least 40 distinct tokens of 256 (Part 9). The share also falls at 4k (54–74%, 35% at batch 64) and 16k (33–54% from batch 2 on), against 58–88% at 1k. Hence, the TD counts are less representative as the context grows, and the 64k ones least. ↩
  7. The DiffusionGemma technical report counts about 84 experts per canvas on PG-19 with its adaptive sampler, i.e., about 17 independent tokens. This is slightly above the range of our batch-1 repeats (32–79 experts at 1k–16k) and equal to our batch-2 count at 1k (84). ↩
  8. Proposition 1 leaves out the vocabulary; the exact accounting at the empirical ceilings, bound (b) below, gives 2.7 under (A5). ↩
